title: The Wealth of Judah and the Garments of the Church
english: My eyes are always toward the Lord.

Similarly, according to the theory applied, one should attempt to take what was said in the Gospel by our Savior, as previously brought forward: 'I came into the world for judgment, so that those not seeing might see and those seeing might become blind' (John 12:47). For the eyes of those seeing sinfully, having been hardened in seeing badly, there will be a dimming regarding seeing rightly and holily.

It is possible also to apply another understanding to the Gospel. Since the Jews, blaspheming the Lord impiously while unfaithfully denying Him, it was fitting that they be blinded, according to what was said in a prophet: 'The servants of God were blinded' (Isa 53:7), those falsely promising to serve Him; and when this happened, those called from the Gentiles into faith rose up, since it had come to pass that he said: 'The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he anointed me, having sent me to preach to the poor, to proclaim release to captives and sight to the blind' (Luke 4:18), having enlightened them with His own wisdom, according to what is written: 'The wisdom of a man lights up his face' (Prov 15:30).

One should also take up what was proclaimed in the Psalms: 'The Lord makes the wise blind' (Ps 146:8), so that they might no longer be shown as blind but as seeing sharply, once the eyes of those seeing wickedly have been hindered and have fallen away from their own pupils—and these are the natural meanings—the eyes that see God. Man raises these eyes toward Him just as he says: 'To You I lifted up my eyes, You who dwell in heaven' (Ps 123:1).

After the flesh has been subdued, whose mindset is enmity toward God, and of those seeing impiously with eyes flowing from the interpreted pupils, so that those seeing sharply may be shown, concerning whom the Apostle writes the word having this expression: 'The eyes of the heart having been enlightened' (Eph 1:18), it is said in harmony that the tongue should also be ordered in the mouth of those having a harmful and material-matter-centered speech, so that what is said by the wise to the Master of all may exist: 'My tongue shall meditate on Your righteousness alone' (Ps 103:2). [Zechariah 14:13-14: And it shall be in that day a great confusion of the Lord upon them, and each will take hold of the hand of his neighbor. And his hand will be joined to the hand of his neighbor...]
Not his. And Judah will array himself in Jerusalem and will gather the strength of all the peoples around him, gold and silver and clothing in a very great multitude.

In the day of the Lord, what the prophet taught was accomplished: a great ecstasy of the Lord upon them, the Lord granting it, the ecstasy here declaring a wonder through negligence and thoughtlessness. For in the prophet Hosea, what is written: 'The sons of Israel shall turn and shall seek the Lord their God and David their king; and they shall stand astonished at the Lord and at His good things' (Hosea 14:2), declares a wonder, or, as some have said, a marvel. Of the same thought exists also that which is written by Habakkuk: 'I have understood your works and was astonished' (Habakkuk 3:2). The prophet says that the ecstasy thus interpreted having come from the Lord upon those being benefited, has become enlarged.

When this happens, 'Judah will array himself in Jerusalem,' concerning which it was said: 'Judah, your brothers praised you,' the Judah who confesses above all. But the receiving Judah arrays himself, confessing in the true Jerusalem, in which 'he who dwells shall not be shaken for ever,' in order to gather around him the strength of all the peoples, gold and silver and a multitude of garments, which is very great.

Often it has been made clear also in other divinely inspired writings, and to the prophet who is set forth for examination, to signify the mind enlightened by the sign of gold and the prudent and exact word by the analogy of silver. Therefore it is appropriate to apply fittingly the gold and the silver and the garments, the great multitude of which the holy Judah has gathered around him from all the peoples, that is, from all those having believed from the nations.

For clothing and garments, according to divine analogy, are the virtues according to kind and the actions performed according to them, and the doctrines of piety and the mysteries of the truth. With these garments she is covered: the bride of Christ, being the Church, and a queen, as it is sung in the forty-fourth and fourth Psalm: 'The queen stood at your right hand, arrayed and adorned in gold' (Psalm 45:13), and adds: 'In embroideries...'

title: The Fall of Horses and Mules
english: Adorned and variegated with gold.

For the Holy Spirit does not teach regarding bodily pleasures to such an extent as to think so, but rather regarding garments that clothe and adorn the inner man, about which it is commanded in Ecclesiastes: 'Let your garments always be white' (Eccl 9:8), which God himself clothes and endows the soul that speaks thankfully: 'I will rejoice in the Lord; for he has clothed me with the garment of salvation and the robe of gladness' (Ps 30:5).

Toward this one swelling with worldly pleasures, the one providing her the same as a bridegroom says: 'I have clothed you in fine linen and purple' (Zech 14:8), fine linen being the beautiful and subtle thoughts and works woven out, and purple being the actions and words of the senses woven together, like the purple growing from the earth, so as to be compared to the sensible things.

Judah, being arrayed as a gathering, seeing the peace of the strong Jerusalem by intellect, gathered the spiritual treasures of the people which are gold, silver, and a great abundance of garments, clearly signifying the mind and the word according to the interpretations by allegory, and the provided clothing being gathered in great abundance. Sufficiently having become clear regarding the present word, we set forth the following to him.
And this shall be the fall of the horses and the mules and the camels and the donkeys and all the cattle that are in those encampments, according to this fall (Zech 14:15).

Just as nations that stood badly have fallen blessedly and risen praiseworthily, as it was correctly interpreted, so the horses, mules, camels, and donkeys according to allegory, having fallen from the position in which they are such, will rise salvationally upon a special good.

For the mares having become those that lust after the mates of their neighbors, they have fallen from the passion of the lover and the state of adultery, in order that they might rise in a praiseworthy resurrection, concerning which Jesus said to those being instructed: 'Arise, let us go from here' (Matt 20:22), and toward the Church having become his bride from the nations he cries: 'Arise, come, my beloved' (Song 2:10). The apostolic [teaching] possesses this understanding here: 'Arise, you who sleep, and rise from the dead' (Eph 5:14)...

"...seeing, and Christ will shine upon you." Similarly to the fall of horses, the mules will also fall, because of a sterility of soul, such as they are called. Concerning both of these animals, the divine Word says to men: "Do not become like the horse and the mule, which have no understanding." (Psalm 147:10). Just as the promiscuous and the many-partnered are called horses, so too a mule might be said allegorically of a virgin possessing an incorrupt body, though not necessarily being holy in the Spirit. Because of such a sterility, even the one who has been castrated is called a mule, not for the sake of the kingdom of heaven, but for the sake of pleasing men.

After the fall, the horses and mules, having been assigned [that role], will rise up and will have the power to charge against those for whom the saints said: "Mount upon your horses, and your cavalry is salvation." (Psalm 147:8). Likewise, the mule will undergo the transformation interpreted by David, whom I call the Savior, riding and charging royally.

In the same manner, the camels and the donkeys and all the other cattle found in those encampments, as is clearly shown, will fall down and rise up. According to the fall of the horses and those called as such, men who study the divine law by rote, but without distinguishing what is to be practiced from what is not, are camels according to tropology.

For indeed, the students of the law, who lift up words by 'nibbling' and devouring 'as if chaff' the pre-laid food, do not break the weapon nor sharpen the claw; they are found to be unclean, not distinguishing the practice from the non-practice. Such are the Jews according to the flesh, who do not divide the Spirit from the letter, nor the truth from the shadow, nor even the things being clearly performed from those being acted out through wickedness, whence it is thus: They are considered a "sinful nation and a people full of sins," because there is not enough for purity from emptiness, that is, to study in vain, according to that which is said concerning them: "The people have studied in vain." (Jeremiah 2:8). For having been born outside the instruction of the one "who begot them and exalted them," all heard as one: "A son who abandons the keeping of his father's instruction will meditate on evil words." (Proverbs 28:7).

title: The Allegory of the Tabernacles
english: a rational form of the Word

Having turned back and having come to it, they ascend annually to worship the Lord King Pantocrator during the time of the feast called the Tabernacles, which the Jews perform for historical reasons and explicitly, as the righteous men were wandering about, and this feast as well as the others.

And first let us see the explicit meaning so that it may be concise and suitable for allegory. Having come out of Egypt, the people of the Hebrews, after the Red Sea had been divided and Pharaoh and all his army had been drowned, the transfer of those helped by God did not happen immediately into the holy land, as all forty years were spent in the wilderness, where there was neither city, nor village, nor houses; and since it was not possible for those about to cross into the holy land to be entirely without dwellings, those who had come out of Egypt raised tents for shelter and habitation, so that they might also in this way have a memory of the existing benefit, by raising tents annually.

The law which was given is a sure witness to this diligence. For it says: 'If your son asks you tomorrow, saying: What are these tabernacles? You shall say to him: We dwelt for a long time in Egypt, and God brought us out of it into this wilderness, and for this reason we raise the tabernacles, so that by seeing them annually, the good gift may by no means be forgotten.'

And how was the feast of the tabernacles performed, and when? 'In the seventh month,' he says, 'on the fifteenth day, take beautiful fruit of the tree, and palm branches, and thick branches, and olive branches, and vine from the stream, to be rejoiced.'

And what does each of these signify for the purpose of following an allegorical interpretation? The tent is described as progress according to virtue and wisdom, being a shelter for those wandering. The theory is made clear in the first and fortieth Psalm, of the one hurrying toward the house of God, saying: 'I will pass through a place of a wonderful tabernacle until the house of God' (Ps 84:1). For a place of a tabernacle and a wonderful progress is necessary for the one passing toward the house of God, dwelling but not yet tabernacling, until having reached the end with much progress, as one might say, in a joyful disposition.
